docs.title: aero-rul
docs.text:
Predict how many flights a turbofan engine has left, with an interval whose coverage is measured on engines the model has never seen.

aero-rul works on NASA's N-CMAPSS dataset, which simulates full flights (climb, cruise, descent) of a fleet of engines until failure. It is a small, tested Python package with one command per step, and every number it reports can be reproduced from a config file.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Step Command Output Read the raw 1 Hz recordings, one row per flight aerorul prepare cycles.parquet Ridge and LightGBM baselines, leave-one-engine-out CV aerorul evaluate baselines.md Prediction intervals and their measured coverage aerorul uncertainty intervals.md, band plots Which sensors the model relies on aerorul explain explain.md, SHAP plot ABC vs random search vs TPE, same budget aerorul benchmark benchmark.md, convergence plot

docs.title: Design choices
docs.text:
• An engine is either in training or in evaluation, never both. Consecutive flights of one engine are nearly identical; splitting by rows would let the model memorise.
  • Uncertainty is measured, not assumed. Conformal intervals come with a guarantee under an exchangeability assumption; we check whether it holds on the test engines.
  • Comparisons are fair or not made. Optimisers get the same budget, space and CV; every result is a mean over seeds.
  • No label leakage. The simulator's hidden health parameters and health-state flag, and the cycle counter, are never model inputs.

See Method for the reasoning behind each choice and Results for the numbers.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
N-CMAPSS (Arias Chao et al., 2021) simulates a fleet of turbofan engines flying until failure under real flight conditions. Each subset is an HDF5 file with a development split and a test split. Every row is one second of flight:

Group Content W flight conditions: altitude, Mach number, throttle resolver angle, fan inlet temperature X_s 14 physical sensors: temperatures, pressures, shaft speeds, fuel flow X_v virtual sensors estimated by the engine model T health parameters, the simulator's hidden degradation state A engine id, flight cycle, flight class, health state Y remaining useful life in flight cycles (the label)

We use DS02, the subset most often used for data-driven prognostics: six development engines (2, 5, 10, 16, 18, 20) and three test engines (11, 14, 15).

docs.title: From seconds to flights
docs.text:
Degradation moves from one flight to the next, not from one second to the next. Each flight cycle becomes one row: for every signal in W and X_s we take the mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum over the flight, plus the flight class and its length. This removes sensor noise and turns millions of rows into a few hundred per engine.

The file is read one engine at a time, so memory use stays at the size of one engine.

docs.title: History features
docs.text: One flight is noisy: weather, payload and route change every reading. Wear shows as a trend. For every per-flight mean and maximum we add the trailing mean and least-squares slope over the engine's last ten flights (fewer at the start of its life). Only the current and earlier flights of the same engine enter a row; a test checks that changing a later flight leaves every earlier row unchanged.

docs.title: What the model may not see
docs.text: Column Why it is excluded unit an identifier, not a property of the engine cycle with a fixed end of life, the flight count nearly gives away the answer hs derived from the simulator's hidden degradation T group the hidden degradation itself

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Consecutive flights of one engine are nearly identical. A random split of rows would put neighbours of every test row into training and report an error the model will never reach on a new engine. We therefore:

  1. cross-validate with leave-one-engine-out on the six development engines, and
  2. report the final score on the three test engines, which no training step touches.

Every number is a mean and standard deviation over five seeds.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
RMSE and MAE are in flight cycles. The NASA scoring function (Saxena et al., 2008) penalises late predictions harder, because predicting more remaining life than there is moves maintenance past the failure. With \(d = \hat{y} - y\):

\[ s = \sum_i \begin{cases} e^{-d_i/13} - 1 & d_i < 0 \\ e^{d_i/10} - 1 & d_i \ge 0 \end{cases} \]

Ten cycles late costs about 1.72; ten cycles early about 1.16. Lower is better.

docs.title: Prediction intervals
docs.text:
A planner needs a range and a statement of how often such ranges are right. We build intervals several ways and measure coverage on the test engines.

Split conformal. Hold out two development engines for calibration and train on the other four. With absolute calibration errors \(r_1, \dots, r_n\), the radius is the \(\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil\)-th smallest error, and the interval is \(\hat{y} \pm q\). If calibration and test points are exchangeable, coverage is at least \(1-\alpha\) for any model.

Cross-conformal. Take the errors from leave-one-engine-out predictions, so every error comes from a model that never saw that engine, and train the final model on all development engines. It uses the data better; its formal guarantee is weaker, which is one more reason to measure coverage directly.

Quantile regression. LightGBM fit to the \(\alpha/2\) and \(1-\alpha/2\) quantiles. Widths adapt to each input, but nothing guarantees coverage.

Conformalized quantile regression (Romano, Patterson and Candès, 2019). The score of a calibration point is how far its true value lies outside the quantile interval, \(E = \max(\hat{q}_{lo} - y,\; y - \hat{q}_{hi})\); the conformal quantile \(q\) of those scores widens (or narrows) the interval to \([\hat{q}_{lo} - q,\; \hat{q}_{hi} + q]\). Scores come from leave-one-engine-out predictions.

Normalised conformal (Lei et al., 2018). Divide each leave-one-engine-out error by a difficulty estimate \(\hat{\sigma}(x)\), take the conformal quantile \(q\) of \(|y - \hat{y}| / \hat{\sigma}(x)\), and return \(\hat{y} \pm q\,\hat{\sigma}(x)\). The guarantee is the same as for cross-conformal, but widths follow the estimated difficulty. Two choices of \(\hat{\sigma}\): a straight line in the predicted RUL (norm_pred, two parameters) and a small LightGBM on the features (norm_feat). The difficulty model for each development engine's score is itself fitted without that engine, and \(\hat{\sigma}\) is floored at a tenth of the mean error so that no point gets a near-zero interval.

Exchangeability

Test engines 14 and 15 fly a different mix of flights from the training engines. If coverage falls short on them, that is evidence of distribution shift, and we report it as a finding rather than tune it away.

docs.title: Maintenance decisions
docs.text:
An interval is only useful if it improves a decision. The decision modelled here: after every flight, book the engine into the shop \(L\) flights ahead (lead time, default 10) as soon as a statistic \(s_t\) of the prediction satisfies \(s_t \le L\). With true remaining life \(r_t\) at the booking flight, the engine fails if \(r_t < L\) and otherwise wastes \(r_t - L\) flights. If nothing triggers, it fails. Cost per engine: waste \(+\,R \times\) failure, with \(R\) the number of wasted flights one unplanned failure is worth, swept from 20 to 200.

Policies differ only in \(s_t\): the point estimate; the point estimate minus a margin tuned on out-of-fold predictions of the training engines for each \(R\); and the lower edge of each 90 % interval. Cross-conformal's lower edge is \(\hat{y} - q\), itself a constant margin, chosen by a coverage target instead of a cost.

Three test engines would give three decisions. The study therefore holds out every engine of DS02 in turn and builds the models, intervals and margins from the remaining eight, with an inner leave-one-engine-out wherever calibration needs it.

docs.title: Hyperparameter search benchmark
docs.text:
We compare three optimisers for LightGBM: the canonical Artificial Bee Colony algorithm (Karaboga, 2005) through abcopt, random search, and Optuna's Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. Everything except the optimiser is fixed: the same seven-parameter search space, the same budget of candidate evaluations, the same leave-one-engine-out objective, five seeds.

abcopt counts every proposal against the budget, including a configuration it has already tried; repeats are served from a cache and cost no compute. If anything this is strict on ABC.

The chosen configuration is refit on all development engines and scored once on the test engines. A better CV score that does not carry over to the test engines means the search overfit the validation engines.

docs.title: Explanations
docs.text: LightGBM computes exact TreeSHAP values. We report mean |SHAP| on the test engines, summed per physical signal. SHAP explains the model, not the engine: correlated sensors share credit, and a high value means the model relies on a signal, not that the signal causes degradation.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Three test engines are few; results are reported per engine as well as pooled.
  • N-CMAPSS is a high-fidelity simulation, not fleet data.
  • Normalised conformal intervals adapt their width but, on DS02, lose coverage near end of life; the default interval therefore has constant width.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: N-CMAPSS DS02: trained on engines 2, 5, 10, 16, 18 and 20 (446 flights), tested on engines 11, 14 and 15 (202 flights). Every number is a mean ± standard deviation over five seeds. Each table is produced by the command named above it.

docs.title: Point prediction
docs.text:
aerorul evaluate

Model Test RMSE Test MAE NASA score per flight CV RMSE LightGBM 10.05 ± 0.43 7.88 ± 0.39 1.66 ± 0.16 10.96 ± 0.09 Ridge 12.75 9.93 2.48 17.06

Test RMSE per engine (LightGBM): engine 11: 9.00, engine 14: 12.87, engine 15: 6.71.

docs.title: Effect of history features
docs.text:
LightGBM Without history With history (10 flights) Test RMSE 10.59 ± 0.25 10.05 ± 0.43 CV RMSE 11.52 ± 0.05 10.96 ± 0.09 CV NASA score per flight 1.91 ± 0.02 1.59 ± 0.03 90 % interval width (cross-conformal) 37.2 34.1

The same features hurt Ridge (CV RMSE 12.91 to 17.06): 146 correlated features on 446 flights overwhelm a lightly regularised linear model.

Reading the per-engine table

Conformal coverage is a guarantee on average over exchangeable points, not for each engine. Engine 14, which also has the largest point error, falls short of 90 %. Pooled coverage alone would hide it.

docs.title: Adaptive (normalised) intervals
docs.text:

Target Method Coverage Width (flights) 90 % Cross-conformal 90.4 % ± 1.5 34.1 90 % Normalised, sigma(prediction) 90.1 % ± 2.2 33.2 90 % Normalised, sigma(features) 99.8 % ± 0.3 56.9 80 % Cross-conformal 78.6 % ± 2.1 25.0 80 % Normalised, sigma(prediction) 79.1 % ± 2.6 24.9 80 % Normalised, sigma(features) 96.8 % ± 2.1 40.7

By phase of life, 90 % target, pooled over engines and seeds (width / coverage):

Method RUL <= 20 20 < RUL <= 50 RUL > 50 Cross-conformal 30.8 / 81.9 % 35.6 / 94.9 % 35.6 / 93.1 % Normalised, sigma(prediction) 21.9 / 74.0 % 35.9 / 97.8 % 42.8 / 96.7 % Normalised, sigma(features) 40.4 / 99.4 % 62.3 / 100 % 68.1 / 100 %

Coverage per test engine at 90 %:

Method Engine 11 Engine 14 Engine 15 Cross-conformal 96.6 % 80.3 % 96.4 % Normalised, sigma(prediction) 98.3 % 77.9 % 96.7 % Normalised, sigma(features) 99.3 % 100 % 100 %

The cross-conformal interval is narrower below 20 flights only because its lower edge is clipped at zero. The normalised interval moves width from the end of life to the start: the marginal guarantee still holds, but coverage drops in the phase a planner cares about most. Conformal guarantees are marginal; they say nothing about coverage within a phase of life, so it has to be measured. The default remains cross-conformal.

docs.title: Maintenance decisions
docs.text:
aerorul decide

Book a removal lead flights ahead once the policy's statistic is at most lead. Failure: less than lead flights left at booking. Waste: life left at removal. Leave-one-engine-out over all nine DS02 engines, five seeds (45 decisions; seeds change the model, not the engines, so this is nine engines' worth of evidence).

Lead time 10 flights, failure rate / wasted flights per engine / mean cost per engine:

Policy Failing Waste Cost, ratio 20 50 100 200 Point estimate 37.8 % 1.7 9.3 20.6 39.5 77.3 Point - tuned margin 11.1 to 26.7 % 3.8 to 9.6 9.1 18.6 20.7 31.8 Quantile regression 26.7 % 1.3 6.6 14.6 28.0 54.6 Cross-conformal 0 % 17.9 17.9 17.9 17.9 17.9 CQR 0 % 10.7 10.7 10.7 10.7 10.7 Normalised conformal 0 % 10.5 10.5 10.5 10.5 10.5

The tuned margin depends on the ratio (mean 3.4, 7.8, 10.5, 10.5 flights); its failure rate and waste change with it. Interval policies do not depend on the ratio.

Only when a failure costs as little as 20 flights of waste does accepting failures pay (quantile regression). For any ratio a real operator would use, the calibrated lower edges win.

Effect of the lead time (failure rate / waste; the tuned margin is left out because it would have to be re-tuned for each lead time):

Policy Lead 5 Lead 10 Lead 15 Lead 20 Point estimate 51.1 % / 1.2 37.8 % / 1.7 48.9 % / 1.1 55.6 % / 1.7 Quantile regression 26.7 % / 1.6 26.7 % / 1.3 42.2 % / 5.0 20.0 % / 12.8 Cross-conformal 0 % / 16.4 0 % / 17.9 0 % / 16.5 0 % / 15.5 CQR 0 % / 7.3 0 % / 10.7 0 % / 28.0 0 % / 39.4 Normalised conformal 8.9 % / 9.1 0 % / 10.5 0 % / 13.3 0 % / 14.3
  • Cross-conformal is the only policy with no failure at any lead time; its price is a steady 16 to 18 flights of waste.
  • Normalised conformal is the cheapest safe policy from 10 flights of lead time upward. At 5 flights it fails engines: the decision then falls in the last flights of life, where its interval was shown to be too narrow.
  • CQR is excellent at short lead times and wasteful at long ones: its lower quantile is conservative early in life.

docs.title: What the model looks at
docs.text:
aerorul explain

Signal Mean |SHAP| (flights of RUL) T50, LPT outlet temperature 16.5 Nc, core speed 5.6 T48, HPT outlet temperature 3.3 P15, bypass duct pressure 2.0 Nf, fan speed 1.9

Fourteen of the fifteen most important features are ten-flight trailing means.

docs.title: Hyperparameter search benchmark
docs.text:
aerorul benchmark

Optimiser Best CV RMSE Seeds won Test RMSE of chosen config Time per search TPE (Optuna) 10.20 ± 0.09 4 / 5 11.04 ± 0.56 135 s Random search 10.31 ± 0.15 1 / 5 11.14 ± 0.94 56 s ABC (abcopt) 10.56 ± 0.17 0 / 5 11.12 ± 1.05 61 s Default parameters 10.96 ± 0.09 10.05 ± 0.43

Budget 60 evaluations, seven hyperparameters, leave-one-engine-out CV on the training engines. TPE finds the lowest validation error, but every tuned configuration does worse on the test engines than the defaults: with six training engines the search fits the validation engines. The released configuration therefore keeps LightGBM's defaults.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install aerorul

or, for development:

git clone https://github.com/yusufkorkmazyigit/aero-rul
cd aero-rul
pip install -e ".[dev]"

docs.title: Data
docs.text: Download the Turbofan Engine Degradation Simulation Data Set-2 (N-CMAPSS) from the NASA Prognostics Data Repository and place N-CMAPSS_DS02-006.h5 in data/raw/. Only this one file is needed. DS02 holds nine engines: units 2, 5, 10, 16, 18 and 20 for development and units 11, 14 and 15 for testing.

docs.title: Run everything
docs.text:
aerorul prepare        # 1 Hz recordings -> one row per flight cycle
aerorul evaluate       # baselines, leave-one-engine-out CV + test score
aerorul uncertainty    # prediction intervals and coverage
aerorul decide         # maintenance policies: failures and wasted life
aerorul explain        # SHAP importance per signal
aerorul benchmark      # ABC vs random search vs TPE (slowest step)

Results are written to results/. Each command reads configs/default.yaml; use --config my.yaml to run another experiment.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
seed: 42
data:
  raw_path: data/raw/N-CMAPSS_DS02-006.h5
  processed_dir: data/processed
features:
  groups: [W, X_s]              # flight conditions + physical sensors
  stats: [mean, std, min, max]  # per-flight summaries of each signal
  rul_cap: null                 # set a number for a piecewise-linear target
  history_window: 10            # trailing mean and slope over the last 10 flights; 0 = off
  history_on: [mean, max]
models:
  names: [ridge, lgbm]
  params: {}                    # e.g. {lgbm: {num_leaves: 15}}
evaluation:
  seeds: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
  results_dir: results
uncertainty:
  model: lgbm
  methods: [split, cv, quantile, cqr, norm_pred, norm_feat]
  alphas: [0.2, 0.1]            # 80 % and 90 % intervals
  calibration_engines: 2
tuning:
  optimizers: [abc, random, tpe]
  budget: 60
  abc_pop_size: 10

Unknown keys are rejected, so a typo fails immediately instead of being ignored.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
pytest

The tests build a small synthetic file with the N-CMAPSS layout, so they need no download.
